strengths: Well-motivated control-theoretic framework with rigorous mathematical foundations (Lemma 3.1, Gramian theory)
Strong empirical validation of key assumptions about HSV stability during training (Figure 2 and appendix figures 5-8)
Model-agnostic method applicable at the dynamical systems level with efficient closed-form solutions for diagonal SSMs (Equation 14)
Comprehensive experimental setup with multiple datasets, 5 random seeds, and both top-1/top-3 reporting
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and logical flow
weaknesses: Fundamental theoretical gap: Section 3.2 explicitly acknowledges that key assumptions (relative ordering stability, bottom-r importance) cannot be guaranteed theoretically and are only empirically validated, undermining claims of principled compression
Highly inconsistent empirical results: method only works on datasets where state dimension correlates with performance (fails on AAN, Pathfinder); no framework to predict when method will help

Limited experimental scope: only LRU architecture tested despite claiming applicability to selective models; no experiments on Mamba or other modern SSMs; missing comparisons with post-training truncation and other in-training compression methods
Modest practical speedup: 4% overhead for 7% accuracy improvement on CIFAR10; computational cost of solving Lyapunov equations (O(n³) for general case) underanalyzed and may offset claimed benefits

Problematic baseline design: models initialized at average final order of compressed models rather than standard small models at target dimension, making it unclear whether improvements come from in-training compression per se vs. appropriate initialization
Incomplete theoretical justification for Linear Time-Varying (selective) case: averaging dynamics over input space (Eq. 19) lacks error analysis and is unvalidated experimentally
Dataset-specific tuning required: IMDB requires special handling (wait 1k steps, different reduction schedule), suggesting method lacks generality
Missing critical comparisons: no experiments comparing in-training vs. post-training balanced truncation; no comparisons with simpler alternatives like training small models from scratch

strengths: Novel application of control-theoretic balanced truncation to in-training neural network compression with solid mathematical foundations (Lemma 3.1, Weyl's theorem)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across six diverse datasets with extensive ablations, timing analysis, and thorough appendix materials demonstrating reproducibility
Strong empirical validation that Hankel singular values remain stable and rank-preserving during training (Figure 2), with proper ablations showing HSV selection strategy matters
Achieves meaningful training speedups (1.5-2.1×) while maintaining or improving accuracy of small models compared to direct training at reduced dimensions
Honest discussion of limitations acknowledging that applicability depends on state-dimension correlation and architecture (SISO vs. MIMO), with extensive treatment of selective SSMs
weaknesses: Limited practical applicability: method only works well when state dimension correlates with performance; fails on datasets like AAN, Pathfinder and struggles with modern SISO architectures (Mamba) that comprise many popular SSMs

Incomplete theoretical justification: while Lemma 3.1 establishes HSV continuity, it doesn't guarantee low-HSV dimensions remain insignificant; claims about stable ordering and bottom-r energy stability are empirically observed but lack theoretical guarantees

Questionable practical benefit: final compressed models remain suboptimal compared to large models (e.g., CIFAR10: 85.7% vs 86.5%, sMNIST: 96.9% vs 97.3%), and speedup gains (1.5-2×) are modest relative to implementation complexity and 5-second JIT overhead per reduction

Selective SSM handling underdeveloped: averaging system matrices (Eq. 22) lacks theoretical justification; mean system stability/controllability not guaranteed; Mamba results show weak state-dimension correlation and poor performance predictability (Table 5: variance of 89.8)

Experimental scope limitations: all experiments on small models (~256 dimensions); no large-scale language modeling tasks where speedups might be more compelling; absence of experiments demonstrating clear advantage over alternatives on domains where state dimension strongly predicts performance
